questions.question: What is Dynamic Programming?
options: A programming paradigm that uses blocks instead of text
An optimization technique that solves complex problems by breaking them into overlapping subproblems and storing their results to avoid recomputation
A brute-force technique that tries all possibilities systematically
A divide-and-conquer technique that never stores intermediate results
questions.explanation: Dynamic Programming solves problems with overlapping subproblems and optimal substructure by caching sub-results (memoization or tabulation) to avoid redundant work.

questions.question: What technique is this and what is its time complexity compared to naive recursion?
options: Tabulation — O(n²) due to the dictionary overhead
Memoization (top-down DP) — O(n) because each subproblem is computed once and cached, vs O(2ⁿ) for naive recursion
Greedy — O(log n) because the cache halves the problem each time
Memoization — still O(2ⁿ) because recursive calls are not eliminated
questions.explanation: This is top-down memoization. The cache ensures each of the n unique subproblems (fib(0) through fib(n)) is computed exactly once — reducing time from O(2ⁿ) to O(n) while using O(n) space for the cache.

questions.question: What is Tabulation?
options: A top-down recursive approach with caching
Documenting algorithm steps in a spreadsheet
A bottom-up DP approach that iteratively fills a table starting from base cases, building up to the target answer
A technique for sorting data into category tables
questions.explanation: Tabulation is bottom-up DP: it fills a table iteratively from the smallest subproblems upward, avoiding recursion and stack overflow risks entirely.

questions.question: Is Memoization top-down or bottom-up?
options: Bottom-up — it starts from the base case and builds upward
Neither — memoization avoids the concept of direction
Top-down — it starts from the main problem and recursively breaks it into subproblems, caching results
Both simultaneously
questions.explanation: Memoization is top-down: the algorithm starts with the full problem, recursively decomposes it, and stores results as subproblems are solved.

questions.question: What is the time and space complexity of this tabulation approach?
options: Time: O(2ⁿ), Space: O(n)
Time: O(n log n), Space: O(1)
Time: O(n) — one loop iteration per value; Space: O(n) — dp array stores n+1 values
Time: O(n), Space: O(1) — no extra storage needed
questions.explanation: The loop runs n times computing each Fibonacci value once → O(n) time. The dp array allocates n+1 slots → O(n) space. This is the standard bottom-up tabulation tradeoff.

questions.question: What is the complexity of naive recursive Fibonacci?
options: O(n) — linear
O(n log n) — linearithmic
O(2ⁿ) — exponential, due to massive redundant recomputation of subproblems
O(n²) — quadratic
questions.explanation: Naive recursive Fibonacci is O(2ⁿ) because it recomputes the same subproblems exponentially — fib(n) calls fib(n-1) and fib(n-2), each of which spawn two more calls, and so on.

questions.question: What is the complexity of DP-optimized Fibonacci?
options: O(2ⁿ) — same as naive recursion
O(n log n) — due to the caching overhead
O(n) — linear, since each subproblem is computed exactly once
O(log n) — because DP halves the problem
questions.explanation: With memoization or tabulation, each of the n Fibonacci values is computed exactly once and stored, reducing complexity from O(2ⁿ) to O(n).

questions.code:
def fib_naive(n):           # called on fib(5)
    if n <= 1: return n
    return fib_naive(n-1) + fib_naive(n-2)

# Call tree for fib(5):
# fib(5) → fib(4) + fib(3)
# fib(4) → fib(3) + fib(2)   ← fib(3) computed AGAIN
# fib(3) → fib(2) + fib(1)   ← fib(2) computed AGAIN
questions.question: What problem does this call tree reveal and what DP property does it violate?
options: No problem — each call computes a different value
Overlapping subproblems — fib(3) and fib(2) are recomputed multiple times, exactly the redundancy DP eliminates through caching
Optimal substructure violation — Fibonacci cannot be solved with DP
Stack overflow — recursion is too deep for any input
questions.explanation: The call tree shows fib(3) computed at least twice and fib(2) at least three times for fib(5) alone. This redundant recomputation of overlapping subproblems is what makes naive recursion O(2ⁿ) — and exactly what memoization/tabulation eliminates.

questions.question: What is the 0/1 Knapsack Problem?
options: A problem of making change with minimum coins
A problem of finding the shortest path in a weighted graph
A problem of selecting a subset of items with given weights and values to maximize total value without exceeding a weight capacity, where each item is either taken (1) or not (0)
A problem of sorting items by their value-to-weight ratio
questions.explanation: 0/1 Knapsack asks: given n items each with a weight and value, which items maximize total value while staying within a weight limit? Each item is binary — included or excluded.

questions.question: Are fractional items allowed in 0/1 Knapsack?
options: Yes, items can be split to fill remaining capacity
Yes, but only for items weighing less than 1 unit
No, each item must be taken entirely or left entirely — no fractions
Fractional amounts are automatically rounded to whole numbers
questions.explanation: The '0/1' in the name means each item is a binary choice: take it completely (1) or don't take it at all (0). This is what prevents a simple greedy solution from working.

questions.question: What are the time and space complexities of this 0/1 Knapsack DP solution?
options: Time: O(n²), Space: O(n)
Time: O(n × capacity), Space: O(n × capacity) — the nested loop fills an (n+1)×(capacity+1) table
Time: O(2ⁿ), Space: O(n × capacity)
Time: O(n log n), Space: O(capacity)
questions.explanation: The nested loops fill every cell of the (n+1)×(capacity+1) DP table once → O(n × capacity) time. The table itself takes O(n × capacity) space. This is the classic pseudo-polynomial complexity of 0/1 Knapsack.

questions.question: What is Longest Common Subsequence (LCS)?
options: The longest string that appears contiguously in both input strings
The longest sequence of characters that appears in the same relative order in both strings, but not necessarily contiguously
The shortest string needed to encode both inputs
The string formed by concatenating both inputs and removing duplicates
questions.explanation: LCS finds the longest sequence present in both strings in the same order — unlike substrings, the characters don't need to be adjacent.

questions.question: Does LCS require letters to be strictly contiguous?
options: Yes, characters must appear consecutively in both strings
Yes, but only in one of the two strings
No, the characters must appear in the same relative order but can be non-contiguous
No, LCS ignores order entirely and just counts shared characters
questions.explanation: LCS characters must appear in the same relative order in both sequences but can be spread out with gaps between them — this makes LCS distinct from Longest Common Substring.

questions.question: What are the time and space complexities of this LCS implementation?
options: Time: O(m + n), Space: O(1)
Time: O(m × n), Space: O(m × n) — both driven by the (m+1)×(n+1) DP table
Time: O(m × n), Space: O(m + n)
Time: O(2^(m+n)), Space: O(m × n)
questions.explanation: The two nested loops each run m and n times respectively, filling every cell of the (m+1)×(n+1) matrix → O(m×n) time. The matrix itself is stored in memory → O(m×n) space.

questions.question: What is the space-time tradeoff?
options: The tradeoff between writing faster code and writing more readable code
The tradeoff where using more memory to store precomputed results can reduce execution time, or vice versa
The tradeoff between using loops and recursion
The tradeoff between time to develop an algorithm and time to run it
questions.explanation: Space-time tradeoff means spending extra memory (e.g., a DP cache or lookup table) to save computation time — DP is the classic example of accepting O(n) or O(n²) space to avoid exponential recomputation.
